13059.title: Equivalent Equations
13059.heading: Equivalent Equations
13059.content:
Equivalent equations have the same solution set even though their expressions differ. Adding the same quantity to both sides or multiplying both sides by the same nonzero quantity produces an equivalent equation.

For example, (3x-5=28), (3x=33), and (x=11) are equivalent. Not every manipulation is reversible on the full domain. Multiplying by an expression that can be zero or cancelling a variable factor may add or remove cases. Recording restrictions and using [[Equation Verification]] protects the equivalence chain.

13062.title: Equivalence Relation
13062.heading: Equivalence Relation
13062.content:
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. It formalizes when different representatives should be treated as describing the same object.

Congruence modulo an integer and equality of cosets are central algebraic examples.

13065.title: Equivalence Principle
13065.heading: Equivalence Principle
13065.content: The equivalence principle states that the local effects of a uniform gravitational field are indistinguishable from those of an accelerating reference frame. An observer in free fall experiences local weightlessness, while an accelerating enclosure can imitate weight. This insight connects gravity to curved spacetime in general relativity.

13068.title: Equivalence Class
13068.heading: Equivalence Class
13068.content:
The equivalence class of an element contains all elements related to it by an [[Equivalence Relation]]. Any member can represent the class, and two classes are either identical or disjoint.

Cosets and residue classes use equivalence classes to construct quotient structures.

13071.title: Equation
13071.heading: Equation
13071.content:
An equation is an assertion that two expressions have equal value. The equals sign records a relationship, not an instruction to calculate only one side.

An [[Algebraic Identity]] is true for every permitted value of its variables, while a [[Conditional Equation]] is true only for particular values. Solving a conditional equation finds those values by producing [[Equivalent Equations]]. The balance must be preserved: an operation applied to one side must be applied compatibly to the other, and any division must respect nonzero restrictions.

13074.title: Equation Verification
13074.heading: Equation Verification
13074.content:
Equation verification substitutes a proposed solution into the original equation and checks whether both sides evaluate to the same value. If (x=11) is proposed for (3x-5=28), then (3(11)-5=28), so it verifies.

Checking the original form matters because later simplified forms may have lost domain restrictions or gained extraneous candidates. Verification also catches arithmetic and sign errors without repeating the entire solution method. A value that fails the check is not a [[Solution of an Equation]], even if it satisfied an intermediate line.

13077.title: Epsilon Neighborhood
13077.heading: Epsilon Neighborhood
13077.content:
An epsilon neighborhood of a point contains observations whose distance from that point is less than a specified positive radius. With Euclidean distance it forms a disk in two dimensions and a ball in three dimensions; other metrics produce different shapes.

Neighborhood radius and metric jointly determine local membership. A radius that is too large can join separate structures, while one that is too small can fragment a coherent group.

13080.title: Epistemic Condition for Moral Responsibility
13080.heading: Epistemic Condition for Moral Responsibility
13080.content:
The epistemic condition for moral responsibility holds that a responsible actor must know, or be in a position where they should know, the morally relevant features and likely consequences of an action. Opaque and complex AI systems can make this knowledge difficult to obtain.

Lack of actual knowledge is not always an excuse. A designer, purchaser, or operator may have a duty to investigate foreseeable risks and understand the limits of a system before relying on it. [[Explainable AI]], testing, documentation, and professional education help actors meet this condition and identify when uncertainty is too great for deployment.

13092.title: Environmental Justice of AI
13092.heading: Environmental Justice of AI
13092.content:
The environmental justice of AI concerns who receives the benefits of intelligent systems and who bears their environmental costs. Energy production, resource extraction, polluted air, discarded hardware, and climate risk are not distributed equally across places or populations.

Wealth can also buy escape from harmful environments through cleaner locations, private infrastructure, or protective technology. An application that benefits affluent users while transferring material damage elsewhere cannot be judged by efficiency alone. Justice requires tracing production and disposal, including affected communities in decisions, and comparing the project with lower-technology alternatives that may be easier to maintain and share.

13095.title: Environmental Impact of AI
13095.heading: Environmental Impact of AI
13095.content:
The environmental impact of AI includes the energy, raw materials, infrastructure, and waste associated with producing and operating data-driven systems. The apparent immateriality of software can hide data centers, devices, electricity generation, extraction, manufacturing, and disposal.

Impact must be evaluated across the system's life rather than only at the point of use. An AI application may improve the efficiency of another process while its own resource demands offset part of the benefit. The distribution of costs also matters because pollution and extraction can burden communities that receive little of the resulting technological value.

13098.title: Enumerative Induction
13098.heading: Enumerative Induction
13098.content:
Enumerative induction infers a generalization from repeated observations of the same kind of event. More confirming instances increase confidence, but repetition alone does not reveal why the relationship holds.

This limitation is central to the classic problem of induction. The source contrasts enumeration with [[Eliminative Induction]], which varies circumstances to identify factors that make a difference.

13104.title: Entropy
13104.heading: Entropy
13104.content: Entropy is a state quantity that measures energy dispersal and, statistically, the number of microscopic arrangements compatible with a macrostate. For reversible heat transfer, $dS=\delta Q_{rev}/T$; statistically, $S=k_B\ln\Omega$. The entropy of an isolated system tends toward a maximum as overwhelmingly probable macrostates are approached.

13107.title: Entity
13107.heading: Entity
13107.content:
An entity is a meaningful value extracted from an utterance to fill an argument of an intent. People, places, dates, quantities, and product names are common entity types.

[[Named Entity Recognition]] locates and labels these spans. The resulting values become slots in a [[Meaning Representation]] that the [[Dialog Manager]] can validate, request, or pass to a service.

13110.title: Entity Relationship
13110.heading: Entity Relationship
13110.content:
An entity relationship states how instances of one persistent entity are associated with instances of another. A city-to-country model, for example, gives each city one country while a country exposes a collection of its cities.

In [[Entity Framework Core]], foreign-key and navigation properties make that relationship available to application code. Conventions or explicit configuration determine how it is represented in the database schema.

13113.heading: Entity Framework Migration
13113.content:
An Entity Framework migration records a change between versions of a code-first data model and expresses the database operations needed to apply or reverse it. Migrations let schema history evolve alongside the application source.

After entities, relationships, or identity structures change, a new migration can be generated and applied to update the database. A migration changes schema; moving existing production data safely may require additional data-migration planning.

13116.title: Entity Invariant
13116.heading: Entity Invariant
13116.content: An entity invariant is a condition that must hold whenever a [[Domain Entity]] completes an operation. Individual [[Value Object]]s can ensure that each input is valid, but the entity must check rules involving combinations of values and its current life-cycle state. For example, an item entering review may require a nonempty title, text, and nonzero price. The operation either produces a valid new state or is rejected, so callers cannot bypass the rule by setting fields directly.

13119.title: Entity Identity
13119.heading: Entity Identity
13119.content: Entity identity uniquely distinguishes one [[Domain Entity]] from all others of the same type throughout its life cycle. It can come from an external domain identifier or be generated by the application, but it should not force construction to depend unnecessarily on a database. A strongly typed identity [[Value Object]] prevents IDs for different entity types from being accidentally exchanged and makes the intended role of a value explicit in method signatures.

13122.content:
Entity Framework Core is an open-source [[Object-Relational Mapping|object-relational mapper]] for .NET applications. It lets application code work with domain-specific object classes while mapping their persistent state to a relational database.

An EF Core model combines entity classes, relationships, conventions, and annotations. A [[Database Context]] coordinates access, a database provider connects the model to a DBMS, and [[Entity Framework Migration|migrations]] translate model changes into schema changes.

13131.heading: ENIAC Plugboard Programming
13131.content:
ENIAC was programmed by wiring its functional units together with cables and setting switches for each problem. Reconfiguring the plugboards could take days even when the resulting computation ran in minutes.

The method matched electronic calculation speed without requiring an unavailable high-speed program memory. Its inflexibility made the need for internally stored instructions unmistakable.

13134.title: Ensemble Learning
13134.heading: Ensemble Learning
13134.content:
Ensemble learning combines predictions from multiple models so their different errors can offset one another. The component learners may be trained on different samples, features, or stages of a procedure.

The combined system can be more accurate or stable than one learner, but its value must be established through evaluation. Additional models also increase computation and can make the final decision harder to explain.

13137.title: ENIAC
13137.heading: ENIAC
13137.content:
ENIAC was a general-purpose electronic numerical machine built by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly for United States Army firing-table calculations. Its roughly 18,000 vacuum tubes performed decimal arithmetic and storage at electronic speed.

The machine demonstrated that ambitious electronic computing could work reliably enough to solve real problems. Its difficult programming method motivated the [[Stored-Program Principle]].

13140.title: Enhanced LORAN
13140.heading: Enhanced LORAN
13140.content: Enhanced LORAN is a proposed modernized terrestrial navigation and timing service based on high-power, low-frequency transmitters. Its signals are much stronger at the receiver than GNSS signals and follow a different propagation path, making it a dissimilar backup that is difficult to jam in the same way. It requires costly ground infrastructure and offers different accuracy and coverage, but those differences are precisely what make it valuable for resilience.

The construct must still retain patient-specific geometry, produce suitable extracellular matrix, and withstand the repeated mechanical loads of joints or other anatomical sites.

13167.title: Engagement
13167.heading: Engagement
13167.content:
Engagement is an ongoing cognitive and emotional state marked by vigor, dedication, and absorption. It persists when a player has reasons to continue attending, acting, learning, and pursuing goals.

Games build engagement through understandable feedback, meaningful decisions, appropriate challenge, and nested interaction loops. [[Fun]] is one positive form of engagement, but a compelling experience can remain engaging without being conventionally fun.

13188.title: Energy Conservation in Thermal Continua
13188.heading: Energy Conservation in Thermal Continua
13188.content:
For any identifiable portion of a continuum, energy entering plus energy generated must equal energy leaving plus energy stored. Applying the balance to progressively smaller elements produces the differential heat equation that relates spatial heat-flux variation to thermal storage and volumetric generation.

The storage term depends on mass, [[Volumetric Heat Capacity|heat capacity]], and the rate of temperature change. At steady state it vanishes, but internal sources and boundary fluxes must still balance; in a transient, their mismatch changes the local temperature field.

The endpoint middleware runs after earlier components such as static-file handling. Its position therefore determines whether a request reaches an [[MVC Controller]], a [[Razor Pages|Razor Page]], or continues to a later single-page-application fallback.

13203.title: Encryption
13203.heading: Encryption
13203.content:
Encryption transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext that conceals the original meaning from a party without the required key. It can protect stored data, transmitted data, or the channel through which communicating endpoints exchange information.

Encryption supports confidentiality but does not by itself establish who created the data, whether an authorized application misused it, or whether every copy was retained appropriately. Key handling and the location at which data is decrypted remain part of the security design.

The encryption process accepts [[Plaintext and Ciphertext|plaintext]] and an [[Encryption Key]] to produce ciphertext; decryption applies the appropriate key to recover the original representation. [[Symmetric Encryption]] and [[Asymmetric Encryption]] make different tradeoffs in speed and key exchange and are often combined in a secure session.

13206.title: Encryption Key
13206.heading: Encryption Key
13206.content:
An encryption key is a value supplied to a cryptographic algorithm to control how data is transformed. The source describes keys as unpredictable bit strings whose length and protection affect the difficulty of recovering protected information.

A strong algorithm cannot preserve confidentiality after its necessary secret keys are stolen. [[Symmetric Encryption]] shares one secret, while [[Asymmetric Encryption]] divides public and private roles between a related key pair.

13209.heading: Encrypted Communication Channel
13209.content:
An encrypted communication channel protects data moving between endpoints from being read or altered easily in transit. The peers establish cryptographic parameters and keys, commonly using an identity certificate to help start a trusted exchange.

Channel encryption protects the route between the participating endpoints. An application may additionally encrypt the data itself when protection must persist after the channel ends or across intermediate systems.

The source describes SSL/TLS session establishment as a client-server exchange in which a certificate is presented and authenticated, supported cipher suites are compared, and keys are exchanged. The established channel combines asymmetric key management with efficient symmetric protection for transmitted data.

13212.title: Encoder-Decoder Network
13212.heading: Encoder-Decoder Network
13212.content:
An encoder-decoder network transforms an input sequence into an internal representation and then generates an output sequence. The encoder reads the source, while the decoder produces the target one step at a time.

The architecture supports mappings whose input and output lengths differ, including speech transcription and language generation. An [[Attention Mechanism]] can let the decoder consult different parts of the encoded input at each step.

Kelleher's sequence-to-sequence translation example uses one LSTM to read source words into a sentence vector and a second LSTM to generate target words. Each generated word is fed back as the next decoder input until an end marker appears. The representation connects two sequences, though a single fixed vector need not capture every nuance of a sentence. The same cross-domain pattern appears in [[CNN-RNN Image Captioning]], where an image encoder supplies the context for a language decoder.

13215.title: ENCODE
13215.heading: ENCODE
13215.content:
ENCODE is a collaborative project that catalogs functional elements in the human genome through many experimental assays and cell contexts. Its shared datasets connect sequence regions with evidence about transcription, regulation, chromatin, and binding.

The project illustrates how standardized metadata, public access, large computational workflows, and integration across experiments support reuse beyond the original study.

This boundary is especially useful when mathematical state has validity conditions. Constructors and controlled mutators can require a schema, prevent illegal parameters, and keep cached summaries synchronized with the underlying records.

13221.title: Empty String
13221.heading: Empty String
13221.content:
The empty string ε is the unique [[String]] containing zero symbols. It has length zero, is its own reversal, and leaves any string unchanged when concatenated on either side.

The empty string is an object, not the absence of a language: {ε} is a one-element language, whereas ∅ contains no strings. ε belongs to every Σ* and to every [[Kleene Star|Kleene closure]].

13224.content:
The empirical rule states that approximately 68.3, 95.4, and 99.7 percent of normally distributed observations lie within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean. A point beyond three standard deviations is therefore rare under normality.

Using the rule for outliers assumes the distribution is approximately normal and that the estimated mean and standard deviation have not been badly distorted by the same extreme cases.

13233.title: Emotional Resonance
13233.heading: Emotional Resonance
13233.content:
Emotional resonance occurs when game events connect with the player's empathy, memory, or sense of consequence. Even simple names, facial expressions, or persistent individual traits can make abstract system states feel like the experiences of characters.

Authored context can give systemic choices emotional weight, while events produced through play can make characters feel personal without a fixed plot. Irreplaceability and accumulated history often strengthen that attachment.

13239.title: Emotional Interactivity
13239.heading: Emotional Interactivity
13239.content:
Emotional interactivity occurs when a player's actions and the game's responses create changing motivations and emotions within meaningful context. It goes beyond momentary startle or sensory pleasure to involve consequences the player cares about.

Authored scenes can target emotion precisely, while systemic emotion is less controllable but can feel more authentic because it follows from [[Player Goal|goals]] and agency. The supporting systems must let player choices genuinely matter.

13245.content:
An emotion design value names the feelings a game should make possible and connects them to the play that may produce them. Tension, tenderness, embarrassment, triumph, uncertainty, grief, or delight require different patterns of action, consequence, timing, and presentation.

The value is an intention rather than a guaranteed output because players bring different histories and interpretations. Playtesting asks whether the designed conditions repeatedly support the emotional direction, not whether every person reports an identical feeling.

13248.title: Emergent Story
13248.heading: Emergent Story
13248.content:
An emergent story is a story about a particular experience of playing a game. It arises as the player learns rules, makes decisions, pursues goals, encounters resistance, and interprets what happened.

The same system can produce different stories for different players or sessions. The range and novelty of those stories depend on the relationships among rules and on how much room the [[Possibility Space]] gives players to develop their own strategies and purposes.

13251.title: Embodied Interaction
13251.heading: Embodied Interaction
13251.content:
Embodied interaction is interaction with computer systems that exist within physical and social reality and make use of that fact. It draws on people's existing experience with physical artifacts, space, time, and social conversation.

Meaning is created, manipulated, and shared through engaged interaction with these embodied phenomena. [[Tangible User Interface|Tangible interfaces]] embody digital information in physical objects, while [[Social Computing]] uses computer systems as a medium or focus for social relationships.

The concept is closely related to [[Activity Theory]] because both treat interaction as something situated in a larger real-world context.

13253.heading: Document

13254.sourceSearchName: emergent biological function emergent biological function
13254.title: Emergent Biological Function
13254.heading: Emergent Biological Function
13254.content:
Emergent biological function is a capability that arises from interactions among cells, materials, and environmental feedback without being specified as one direct design step. Living components can reorganize and adapt after fabrication.

The possibility requires monitoring and revision because a construct may become stronger, more connected, or behaviorally different from the state originally reviewed for safety.

13257.title: Emergence
13257.heading: Emergence
13257.content:
Emergence is the appearance of a relatively stable property or behavior at the level of a whole that is qualitatively different from the properties of its individual parts. It is produced by distributed interactions rather than directed by one component.

Local, generic [[Modular Behavior|behaviors]] and feedback loops make emergence possible. The resulting whole can in turn affect its parts through [[Downward Causality]], while the parts create it through [[Upward Causality]].

In games, emergence can appear as a strategy, event, or story that no author explicitly sequenced. It arises from the player's choices interacting with the system and may differ substantially between sessions using the same rules.

13260.title: Embodied Intelligence
13260.heading: Embodied Intelligence
13260.content:
Embodied intelligence is the view that intelligent action depends on having a body that perceives and acts within a material environment. Knowledge is not exhausted by stored propositions or formal rules; it also develops through situated coping, movement, and practical engagement.

This view challenges accounts of intelligence as abstract symbol processing alone. A machine can manipulate representations without sharing the bodily needs, vulnerabilities, and practical situations that give human concepts relevance. Embodiment does not prove that intelligent machines are impossible, but it changes the design question from reproducing detached reasoning to coordinating perception, action, environment, and learned skill.

13269.heading: Embedded Prime
13269.content:
An embedded prime is an [[Associated Prime]] that is not minimal among the associated primes of a module. It represents a component contained inside the support associated with a smaller prime.

In a primary decomposition, minimal associated primes describe isolated components, while embedded primes reflect additional algebraic structure that is not a separate minimal component of the underlying support.

13272.title: Embedded QA
13272.heading: Embedded QA
13272.content:
Embedded QA places a tester within a cross-discipline team so testing knowledge participates in planning, acceptance criteria, implementation feedback, regression work, and tool improvement. This shortens the delay between creating and understanding a defect.

A centralized test pool can still supplement the team as scale and platform complexity grow. Embedding changes when quality expertise enters decisions, not who alone owns quality.

13278.title: Embedded JPEG Thumbnail
13278.heading: Embedded JPEG Thumbnail
13278.content:
An embedded JPEG thumbnail is a small preview stored in an image's metadata. A camera typically creates it from the full image through a device-specific sequence of resizing, filtering, enhancement, and JPEG encoding, with characteristic dimensions and compression choices.

The preview is a second representation of the captured scene and can preserve evidence overlooked during editing. If the full-size pixels change while the thumbnail remains untouched, the two may depict different content; if software regenerates it, its dimensions and encoding may instead reveal the new pipeline.

13281.title: Embedded Feature Selection Model
13281.heading: Embedded Feature Selection Model
13281.content:
An embedded feature selection model chooses variables as part of classifier fitting rather than as a separate preprocessing search. The selection decision and estimation of predictive parameters occur together.

The source presents embedded selection as a bridge between fast filter scoring and accurate wrapper evaluation. Sparse penalties and tree split selection are typical mechanisms through which a learning objective can suppress unnecessary variables while fitting the model.

Embedded methods can exploit the learning algorithm's internal structure while avoiding a separate wrapper search. The selected subset is consequently tied to the model objective, regularization, and fitting procedure.

That integration can be computationally favorable for large datasets because selection occurs during a fit that was already required. Scalability still depends on whether the learning algorithm itself can be distributed or adapted to streaming data.

13284.heading: Embedded CSS Style Sheets
13284.content:
An embedded stylesheet places CSS rules inside a document's `style` element. The rules apply to that document without requiring a separate CSS file, and a `media` attribute can restrict them to selected output media.

Embedding keeps the rules near the markup but limits their reuse. It is broader than [[Inline CSS Styles]], because selectors in the embedded sheet can match any appropriate element in the document.

13287.title: Elliptical Utterance
13287.heading: Elliptical Utterance
13287.content:
An elliptical utterance omits words whose meaning can be recovered from context. After asking about restaurants in Boston, a user might say “How about Cambridge?” without restating the full request.

The [[Dialog Manager]] combines the fragment with [[Conversation Context]] to reconstruct the intended [[Meaning Representation]]. Treating the utterance in isolation would often produce an incomplete or incorrect intent.

13290.heading: Elliptical Orbits and Kepler's Laws
13290.content: Kepler's first law describes an orbit as an ellipse with the parent body at one focus. The second law states that the line from parent to orbiter sweeps equal areas in equal times, so orbital speed varies around the ellipse. The third law relates the square of orbital period to the cube of orbital size, connecting geometry to [[Orbital Velocity and Period]].

13293.title: Eliminative Induction
13293.heading: Eliminative Induction
13293.content:
Eliminative induction compares cases under varied circumstances to rule out candidate explanations and isolate relationships that may be causal. It seeks informative differences rather than relying only on the repeated presence of a pattern.

The approach better resembles experimental and observational scientific practice than simple enumeration. Its conclusions remain revisable as new variations and evidence test previously unexamined alternatives.

13296.title: Elimination Theorem
13296.heading: Elimination Theorem
13296.content:
The elimination theorem states that if G is a Gröbner basis in lexicographic order x₁ > ··· > xₙ, then the elements of G involving only xₗ₊₁,…,xₙ form a Gröbner basis for the ℓ-th [[Elimination Ideal]].

The theorem turns variable removal into basis selection after one computation. Its geometric counterpart describes the Zariski closure of a projected affine variety.

13299.title: Elimination Ideal
13299.heading: Elimination Ideal
13299.content:
For an ideal I in K[x₁,…,xₙ], the ℓ-th elimination ideal is I ∩ K[xₗ₊₁,…,xₙ]. It contains exactly the consequences of I that do not involve the first ℓ variables.

Computing a Gröbner basis in lexicographic order exposes this intersection through the [[Elimination Theorem]]. Elimination ideals describe projections and produce implicit equations from parametrizations.

13302.title: Eliminating Intuition from Routine Computation
13302.heading: Eliminating Intuition from Routine Computation
13302.content:
The historical effort to mechanize calculation aimed to remove intuition from routine execution. Experts translated their practiced judgments into explicit steps so that repetitive work could be performed consistently by less experienced people or by machines.

This did not make intuition worthless. Expert intuition remained essential for finding the core of a problem, choosing a method, noticing anomalies, and deciding when a formal routine no longer fit the situation.

13305.heading: Elementary Row Operation
13305.content:
An elementary row operation interchanges two rows, multiplies a row by a nonzero scalar, or adds a multiple of one row to another.

Applied to an [[Augmented Matrix]], these operations preserve the solution set of its [[Linear System]]. Each operation is equivalent to left multiplication by an [[Elementary Matrix]].

13308.title: Element Stiffness Matrix
13308.heading: Element Stiffness Matrix
13308.content:
An element stiffness matrix relates an element's nodal response vector to its nodal load vector. Its coefficients depend on the element geometry, material properties, interpolation model, and governing physics.

Although “stiffness” comes from structural mechanics, an analogous characteristic matrix appears in thermal, fluid-potential, and electromagnetic problems. Assembly maps each local coefficient into the global equation system.

13311.title: Elementary Matrix
13311.heading: Elementary Matrix
13311.content:
An elementary matrix is obtained by applying one [[Elementary Row Operation]] to an [[Identity Matrix]]. Left multiplication by it performs the same row operation on another matrix.

Every elementary matrix is invertible, and its inverse corresponds to undoing the row operation. A [[Nonsingular Matrix]] can be represented as a product of elementary matrices.
